title: Kamindu guides Kaps to crucial LPL win - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
July.30 (Mirror Sports) - Colombo Kaps boosted their Lanka Premier League 2026 playoff hopes after holding their nerve to defeat Dambulla Sixers by four wickets in a high-scoring contest at the Pallekele International Cricket Stadium on Wednesday

Set a target of 175, the Kaps attacked from the outset through Rubin Hermann, whose aggressive 48 from 26 balls put the chase firmly on track. Captain Kamindu Mendis then produced a calm 39 to steady the innings before Ben McDermott (33) and Sadeera Samarawickrama (26) combined to carry Colombo over the line with six balls remaining.

The Sixers had earlier built a competitive total of 174 for 5 after another classy display from Reeza Hendricks. The South African opener struck 80 from 54 deliveries, registering his third fifty of the tournament, while Gulbadin Naib's unbeaten 33 from just 13 balls gave Dambulla a late surge. Shahnawaz Dahani finished as Colombo's most successful bowler with two wickets.

Dambulla fought back through Dushmantha Chameera and Akila Dananjaya, who claimed two wickets each, but the Kaps held their composure to seal an important victory and keep their momentum alive in the race for the knockout stage.

Brief Scores

Dambulla Sixers – 174/5 (20 overs)

Reeza Hendricks 80 (54), Gulbadin Naib 33* (13), Sikandar Raza 23; Shahnawaz Dahani 2/41.

Colombo Kaps – 177/6 (19 overs)

Rubin Hermann 48 (26), Kamindu Mendis 39, Ben McDermott 33, Sadeera Samarawickrama 26; Dushmantha Chameera 2/32, Akila Dananjaya 2/32.

Result: Colombo Kaps won by four wickets.

title: Palestinian tourist killed in parasailing accident off Bentota - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Bentota, July 29 (Daily Mirror): A 31-year-old Palestinian woman was killed after a parasail reportedly crashed into the sea off the Bentota coast this evening (29), police said.

According to Bentota Police, the accident occurred when a parasail operated by an organisation based along the Bentota coastal road plunged into the sea during a flight.

The Palestinian tourist, who was on board the parasail, died in the incident, while the operator, a Colombian national, survived.

The victim's body has been placed at the Nagoda Hospital mortuary for a post-mortem examination.

Bentota Police have launched an investigation to determine the exact cause of the accident.

title: Reclaiming the Republic: Why True Judicial Efficiency Demands Systemic Reform Over Retirement Age Extensions - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
2/3 Majority vs. Republicanism: Numbers Do Not Equal Right

By Attorney at Law, Namini Panditha, Founder, Liberal youth Movement

A fundamental mistake in political thinking is confusing a raw democratic majority with a true constitutional republic. Securing a two-thirds majority in Parliament grants a government the legal authority to pass legislation, but it does not give it the moral authority to rewrite the rules of governance at will.

In a pure democracy, majoritarian power can quickly become numbers-driven control, where 66% of lawmakers can override fundamental principles simply because they have the votes. In contrast, republicanism is built on the principle that certain values—such as the rule of law, the separation of powers, and institutional checks and balances—are higher than any majority. The judiciary exists specifically to protect individual rights and the Constitution from majoritarian overreach. When a government uses its raw parliamentary numbers to alter judicial structures mid-stream, it elevates majoritarian force above republican values.

The Right Way to Amend a Constitution

A constitution is meant to be a stable framework, not a draft document that changes whenever a new administration takes office. For a constitutional amendment to be legitimate, it must follow two essential principles:

1. Prospective Application: Any change to judicial service conditions or retirement ages must apply only to future appointees who take office after the law is passed. Applying extensions to sitting judges creates an unavoidable appearance of political patronage.

2. The "Veil of Ignorance": Sound governance requires lawmakers to write structural rules as if they do not know whether they will be in power or in opposition when those rules take effect.

If an extension applies to current judges, it changes the rules mid-game. Even if done with no ill intent, it creates a subtle incentive structure where judges approaching retirement could be perceived as aligning with the executive to secure an extension.

What History Teaches Us: The Trap of Ad-Hoc Amendments

Sri Lanka’s political history offers a clear, repeated warning about tailoring constitutional rules to suit immediate circumstances. Successive governments have used their parliamentary majorities to pass ad-hoc amendments to solve short-term administrative or political challenges:

• The 18th Amendment (2010) removed presidential term limits to consolidate executive control.

• The 20th Amendment (2020) recentralized power over independent commissions and the judiciary.



History shows a consistent outcome: every regime that tampered with constitutional safeguards to entrench its authority ultimately suffered severe public backlash and lost power. The electorate inevitably rejects governments that manipulate state institutions for political convenience. Short-term institutional fixes routinely lead to long-term political failure.

Values Matter More Than What the Majority Says

Democratic legitimacy does not come from parliamentary strength alone; it comes from adherence to foundational principles. The independence of the judiciary is not an abstract concept—it relies entirely on public trust.

For justice to function, the courts must not only be independent; they must be seen to be independent. When a government uses its majority to alter judicial tenures, it weakens public trust in the neutral administration of justice. Once public confidence in the courts is eroded, no parliamentary majority can restore it. Enduring institutional values must always take precedence over temporary political power.

Good Intentions, Bad Outcomes

Reforms driven by administrative efficiency can still lead to damaging consequences if core institutional boundaries are crossed. A government may argue that extending judges' terms retains experienced legal minds or helps clear court backlogs.



However, when a good intention is executed by departing from constitutional norms, the systemic damage far outweighs the short-term benefits. This can create a precedent that future administrations can exploit. Good intentions cannot cure a flawed process.

Bad Intentions, Bad Outcomes: The Paradox of Political Opposition



When controversial amendments are introduced, much of the political opposition does not stem from a principled commitment to the rule of law. Often, opposition figures attack the proposal purely for political advantage despite having enacted similar or worse constitutional manipulations when they were in power.

The public recognizes this hypocrisy. When politicians who previously weakened judicial independence suddenly present themselves as guardians of the Constitution, their arguments carry little weight. This creates a dangerous cynicism where citizens distrust both the government proposing the change and the opposition criticizing it.

Breaking the Cycle: A Call for Consistency

The current administration has an opportunity to break this historical cycle and avoid setting precedents that it would object to if placed in opposition in the future. If a policy decision is made to raise the retirement age of judges, the state can still enact this extension provided it applies strictly to future appointees. True judicial efficiency is not achieved through tenure extensions for sitting judges, but through deliberate, foundational steps: building widespread public legal awareness, strengthening legal education, encouraging Public Interest Litigation (PIL), expanding the legal aid system, depoliticizing key state institutions including the police, and allocating significantly more funds toward these priorities in the national budget. By prioritizing these structural efforts, the government can modernize the legal system while safeguarding the foundational integrity of the Constitution.

title: Private hospital fined Rs. 500,000 for overcharging on blood test - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
A private hospital in Vavuniya has been fined Rs. 500,000 for charging above the government-controlled price for a Full Blood Count (FBC) test.

According to the Consumer Affairs Authority (CAA), the violation was detected during a raid conducted by its investigation officers, who found that the hospital had overcharged patients for the laboratory test in breach of the regulated pricing.

Following the investigation, the Authority filed legal action against the hospital before the Vavuniya Magistrate’s Court.

After hearing the case, the Vavuniya Magistrate’s Court imposed a fine of Rs. 500,000 on the private hospital for violating the government-controlled price regulations, the CAA said.

title: BASL unanimously passes resolution against proposed judges’ retirement age amendment - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary: The Special General Meeting of the General Membership of the Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) today unanimously passed a resolution strongly opposing the proposed amendment to increase the retirement age of judges.

title: BASL was not consulted on proposed judges’ retirement age amendment: BASL President - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) President Rajeev Amarasuriya today said the BASL had not been consulted before the Government proceeded with the proposed constitutional amendment seeking to extend the retirement age of judges.

Addressing the BASL’s Special General Meeting of the General Membership, Amarasuriya said the proposed amendment had been presented to the Cabinet and approved a few days ago without any prior consultation with the Bar Association.

He made the remarks while addressing a large gathering of members at the BASL headquarters in Hulftsdorp, where the proposed constitutional amendment on the retirement age of judges was being discussed.

title: Iran to get Chinese shoulder-launched missile systems in weeks: Reuters
summary: Iran is expected to receive within weeks a first shipment out of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defence missile launchers, three sources familiar with the deal told Reuters, as it rebuilds its defences amid war with the United States.

title: BASL special general meeting begins amid large lawyer turnout - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Colombo, July 29 (Daily MIrror) - The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) Special General Meeting of its General Membership commenced a short while ago at the BASL Head Office in Hulftsdorp, with a large number of lawyers in attendance.

The government’s proposed constitutional amendment seeking to extend the retirement age of judges will be discussed at the Special General Meeting.

title: Technical fault delays KKS Intercity train; passengers face inconvenience - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Passengers travelling on the Kankesanthurai (KKS) Intercity Express faced delays and overcrowding today after the train developed a technical fault at the Veyangoda Railway Station.

The train had departed Colombo Fort Railway Station at 5.45 a.m. and encountered the technical fault at around 8.00 a.m., railway sources said.

As today was a Poya Day, all seats on the train had been fully reserved. Passengers were subsequently transferred to the Yal Devi Express, which arrived behind the disabled train, allowing them to continue their journey.

However, the transfer resulted in passengers from both trains travelling on a single service, causing severe overcrowding and inconvenience.

Meanwhile, the faulty Kankesanthurai Intercity Express remained at the Veyangoda Railway Station.

To assist passengers who were waiting at Veyangoda and the subsequent railway stations, the Railway Department operated a replacement train from Veyangoda to Kankesanthurai at 10.30 a.m.

title: BASL to hold special General Meeting on proposed judicial retirement age increase - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Colombo, July 29 (Daily MIrror) - The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) will convene a Special General Meeting in Colombo today (29) to discuss the government's proposed move to increase the retirement age of judges.

BASL President, Attorney-at-Law Rajeev Amarasuriya, said the meeting, scheduled to begin at 11:00 a.m. at the BASL premises, will focus on determining the association's response to the proposal.

Amarasuriya said that the matter is not related to any individual judge but concerns the independence of the judiciary, constitutional principles, and public confidence in the justice system. He said that any constitutional amendment of this nature should only be introduced following broad public and stakeholder consultation, with full transparency and due process.

He also called on all members of the Bar Association of Sri Lanka to attend the meeting and take part in discussions on what he described as an important national issue.

title: Japan quake toll rises to 13 as rescuers haul people from collapsed mall
summary: Rescuers were frantically searching on Wednesday for survivors of a 7.1-magnitude earthquake that shook southern Japan, killing at least 13 people, knocking out power to thousands of homes and rupturing roads across the region.

title: Anti-Corruption Unit constable dead in apparent suicide - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Panadura, July 29 (Daily Mirror) - A police constable has died by suspected suicide after shooting himself with his official service firearm.

According to the police, the deceased officer was attached to the Panadura Walana Anti-Corruption Strike Unit.

The incident occurred early this morning (29) near the main gate of the police station, where the constable allegedly shot himself using his T-56 assault rifle.

After sustaining critical injuries in the shooting, the officer was admitted to the Panadura Base Hospital, where he subsequently succumbed to his injuries.

Police said the deceased was a 28-year-old resident of the Peradeniya area.

title: Company director arrested over alleged housing investment scam - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Colombo, July 29 (Daily MIrror) - A director of a private company has been arrested by the Mirihana Special Crimes Investigation Division for allegedly defrauding members of the public by promising houses and land under an easy payment scheme.

According to police, the suspect promoted the scheme through advertisements on social media, claiming that customers could obtain houses and land through affordable payment plans. Victims were reportedly required to sign agreements and pay an advance amount equivalent to 60% of the total value of the house and land.

Investigations revealed that after collecting the advance payments, the suspect allegedly failed to construct or deliver the promised houses. Customers who later requested refunds were reportedly issued cheques that were subsequently dishonoured.

The suspect is a 48-year-old resident of Negombo.

Police said the Mirihana Special Crimes Investigation Division has so far received five complaints in connection with the alleged fraud, while additional complaints from other affected individuals are expected.

The suspect was produced before the Nugegoda Magistrate's Court on July 28 and was remanded until August 4.

Further investigations are being conducted by the Mirihana Special Crimes Investigation Division.

title: Australia’s Gold Rush, Seales’ heroics, Essex history & UEFA oppose FIFA plan - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
July.29 (Mirror Sports) - From medal dominance to cricket heroics, historic milestones and football controversies, the world of sport produced another action-packed day. Australia, West Indies, Essex Cricket and UEFA all made headlines in the latest global sports roundup.

- Australia Tops Glasgow 2026 Medal Table

Australia continues to dominate the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, leading the medal table with 35 gold, 18 silver and 27 bronze medals as of 29 July.

The Australian team has built a strong advantage across multiple sports, securing the top position ahead of its Commonwealth rivals. With more events still to come, Australia remains on course to extend its lead and strengthen its position as the most successful nation at the Games.

- Seales Stars as West Indies Defeat Pakistan in First Test

Jayden Seales claimed five wickets as West Indies defeated Pakistan by 90 runs in the first Test at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy in Trinidad. The victory gave the hosts a 1-0 lead in the two-match series.

Chasing 211 for victory, Pakistan were bowled out for 120 after a late fightback from Babar Azam, who remained unbeaten on 58. Seales finished with figures of 5-20, while Justin Greaves also played a key role with his brilliant bowling performance.

West Indies captain Roston Chase dedicated the win to the late Sir Garfield Sobers, saying the team wanted to honour the legendary cricketer with a memorable performance. The second Test will begin in Port of Spain on August 2.

West Indies 311 (Hope 92; Ali 4-50) & 181 (Joseph 38; Abbas 5-22)

Pakistan 282 (Masood 109; Greaves 5-27) & 120 (Azam 58*; Seales 5-20)

West Indies won by 90 runs; lead series 1-0

- Essex Appoint Rachel Lewis as First Female Chair

Essex Cricket have appointed Rachel Lewis as the club’s first-ever female chair of the board in their 150-year history. Lewis replaces Jason Gallian, who stepped down from the role after “careful consideration” last week.

The former Olympic volleyball player has served as chairwoman of Essex Cricket in the Community for the past three years and becomes the club’s fifth chair in five years.

Lewis said she was excited to lead the club into a new era, with Essex focused on ground redevelopment and continued success for both their men’s and women’s teams. Gallian will remain involved as a board member.

- UEFA Hits Out at FIFA Investment Plan

UEFA and Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham have criticised FIFA’s plan to bring private investment into its competitions, including the FIFA World Cup. FIFA said the move aims to boost football development funding beyond $10 billion through a new commercial subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise.

The proposal would allow third-party investors to take minority stakes in the venture, with US firm Thrive Eternal expected to lead the investor group. The plan still needs approval from FIFA’s 211 member associations.

UEFA said the move “crosses a line”, while Burnham warned that football should not be controlled by investors. He insisted the game belongs to fans and communities rather than commercial interests.

title: Sri Lanka pharma sets sights on US$ 1.8tn global market - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Dinesh Athapaththu

Nalin Kannangara

By Nishel Fernando

Sri Lanka’s pharmaceutical manufacturing industry is pushing to evolve from an import-substitution model into a multi-billion dollar export engine, eyeing a slice of the US$ 1.8 trillion global market.

Speaking at the Annual General Meeting of the Sri Lanka Pharmaceutical Manufacturers’ Association (SLPMA) held in Colombo this week, industry leaders outlined a bold vision to transform the sector into the country’s next thrust industry. By capitalising on an abundant pool of high-quality science graduates and strategic regional proximity, manufacturers believe Sri Lanka can carve out a highly specialized, globally competitive export niche.

A central pillar of this ambition relies on harnessing the talent generated by the state’s free education system. Newly elected SLPMA President Dinesh Athapaththu emphasised that the sector could effectively absorb thousands of science graduates who currently migrate or remain underemployed in roles below their capacity. Pointing to the massive scale of the global pharmaceutical arena, he noted that capturing even a fraction of it would secure a sustainable economic future.

Addressing concerns regarding regional competition, he stated, “It is not a comparative advantage that we are going to have with India. We should not consider a comparative advantage with India, and it’s all about how we can create a competitive advantage”.

The industry has already undergone a massive transformation over the past decade. Outgoing SLPMA President Nalin Kannangara noted the sector now operates 25 manufacturing facilities compliant with World Health Organization Good Manufacturing Practice standards, producing over 300 local products. These manufacturers currently meet 45 percent of the Medical Supplies Division’s requirements, a significant increase from just 10 percent a decade ago. This growth in the state sector was largely driven by crucial government buyback agreements. However, despite this strong public sector footprint, local manufacturers currently hold a mere 5 percent market share in the highly competitive private sector.

This robust domestic foundation is increasingly prompting successful manufacturers to target international expansion. A prime example is Morison Limited, the pharmaceutical manufacturing arm of Hemas Holdings PLC, which is aggressively laying the groundwork for a major export drive after reaching a critical mass in the domestic healthcare sector. Having invested Rs. 4 billion into a state-of-the-art manufacturing and research facility in Homagama, the company is currently undergoing the rigorous European Union Good Manufacturing Practice (EU-GMP) certification process. This strategic outward pivot is designed to open access to highly regulated international markets and position the homegrown manufacturer as a competitive player in global supply chains, helping to mitigate local macroeconomic vulnerabilities.

To replicate this success on a national scale, manufacturers are urging the government to clear severe policy and regulatory roadblocks. A primary grievance is the uneven playing field that heavily taxes research and development. While imported finished pharmaceuticals enter Sri Lanka tax-free, local manufacturers importing raw materials for trials, formulation, and validation batches are subjected to an 18 percent Value Added Tax, a 5 percent Ports and Airports Development Levy, and a 2.5 percent Social Security Contribution Levy.

Warning that “our product development cost will go overboard,” Kannangara explained that these taxes effectively stifle innovation and make locally manufactured products uncompetitive against foreign imports.

Expressing his frustration over the failure to resolve the taxation issues on packaging materials despite repeated requests, Kannangara quipped, “I ended up with a nickname called VAT Mac,” and added, “I have no option but to pass down this challenge to the new president”.

Furthermore, the local market is currently facing an influx of cheap pharmaceutical imports triggered by Maximum Retail Price caps. The local industry has raised concerns over the lack of adequate testing facilities to ensure the quality of these cheap imports flooding the country, putting both patients and local competitiveness at risk.

Bureaucratic red tape further compounds these financial strains, severely delaying the crucial product development cycle. Every raw material consignment currently requires a tedious debited letter process routed through the Health Ministry, the National Medicines Regulatory Authority (NMRA), and Customs. Achieving export readiness requires policymakers to understand the industry’s complex and highly capital-intensive investment cycle. Outlining the grueling timelines, Athapaththu explained that building a pharmaceutical facility takes four to five years, followed by a year of qualification and validation. After the plant is ready, complex product development takes another 18 months, followed by at least a year for registration. Because the return on investment is a long-haul game, he noted that “your export process starts just after getting into the Sri Lankan market,” demanding immense investor patience and a highly supportive local ecosystem.

To survive the long road to profitability, the industry is demanding a dedicated, fast-tracked registration channel at the NMRA and the immediate rationalisation of taxes on research materials. Furthermore, manufacturers are calling for a strategic extension of the government buyback guarantee until 2030, providing the financial stability needed to anchor local investments before launching into the global export arena.

Emphasising the need for support, Athapaththu argued, “We should consider buybacks as a transitional arrangement”.
